items.title: Developers have optimized over 100,000 apps for the iPhone Duo
items.content_html:
Apple says that developers have been rapidly adapting their apps for the iPhone Duo's twin screens, with thousands of new ones being added daily.

The lack of apps that hadn't been updated for the iPhone Duo was definitely the device's Achilles' heel. But as AppleInsider said, that problem was small, getting smaller, and by the time most buyers get their iPhone Duo, it will be gone.

Now in a statement to AppleInsider, Apple has boasted about the rate at which developers are updating to take advantage of the iPhone Duo.

"It's been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we're grateful for their creativity and innovation," Susan Prescott, Apple's vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations. "Today there are well over 100,000 apps built for iPhone Duo already live on the App Store, and thousands of optimized apps are being added to the store each day."

Prescott made similar remarks in late October 2026, but since then has added more detail about how Apple is working with developers.

"In the last month alone, thousands of developers have joined us for workshops in 19 cities around the world to experience iPhone Duo firsthand and bring updated apps to their users," she said. "The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we're excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo."

Separately, a particularly notable update for the iPhone Duo has been from Google. Larger firms such as Google and Microsoft have often been very late to adopting new Apple requirements, but Google has rapidly updated its Maps app.

Why apps need updating

If developers have consistently followed Apple's recommendations, then their apps already make some use of the iPhone Duo's two screens. But to fully use the width of both the external and internal screens, developers need to do some work.

How the updated Google Maps uses the whole of the inner and outer displays on the iPhone Duo.

Apple says that this extra work is minor. But if developers have not been following those recommendations, then the effort needed is much more substantial.

It's also much more important, too. Such apps are shown in the center of the inner screen with large black bars to left and right.

Users can expand the app to more or less fill the screen, but it looks poor. Plus users can drag such an app to one side of the screen or the other, and then open a second app to fill up the rest of the screen.

But then beyond their appearance, apps that have been properly updated for the iPhone Duo make extra use of the device's form factor. Apps can tell how wide open the device is, for instance, and adjust their controls to best serve the user.

items.title: iPhone 20 range rumored to ditch Action Button
items.content_html:
The Action Button may soon be dropped, but if you thought that would mean getting back the much-missed mute switch, think again.

Back in 2023, the Action Button began replacing the mute switch on ever iPhones, but that stopped with the launch of the iPhone Duo. Now prolific leaker Instant Digital claims that it's about to be history.

Writing on the Chinese social media site Weibo, they say (in translation) that "Apple's Action button... will officially be phased out starting with new iPhone models in the second half of next year." So presuming Apple sticks to its new split iPhone launch, that may mean that the 20th anniversary iPhone will be the first to lose it.

"It will be integrated with the camera button," the leaker continues. "Tap to launch the camera, press and hold... to perform [the Action Button's] function."

The camera button referred to is presumably the iPhone's Camera Control. This already launches the camera with one tap, but pressing longer is already a way to use Visual Intelligence.

If correct, the Action Button would be the first iPhone control to be removed since that button replaced the mute switch.

While it's unusual for Apple to do this, the company must know how much or how little it is used. Whatever the figures are, they weren't high enough to make finding space for the Action Button on the iPhone Duo a priority.

Then there is also that the button and what its settings are hasn't been significantly updated since launch. There is still the peculiar design that pressing it once does nothing but display a notice telling you to press longer.

Nonetheless, pressing and holding has proved a quick enough way to launch one action or, via Shortcuts, multiple ones. But, speaking of Shortcuts, it is already possible to emulate practically every benefit of the Action Button with a lock screen icon.

The Action Button was first introduced on the Apple Watch Ultra.

Note that Weibo leakers do not have a great track record. Instant Digital has sometimes posted what seems more like wishful thinking than an actual leak.

Even so, removing the Action Button does seem plausible given its absence on the iPhone Duo.

Apple had hopes for the Action Button

The Action Button first appeared on the Apple Watch Ultra back in September 2022. Then it came to the iPhone with the iPhone 15 Pro the following year and the smart money would've bet on it coming to the iPad eventually.

It never did, but Apple certainly had more plans for the Action Button, at least at one stage.

In 2024, for instance, a patent revealed that there could even be more than one Action Button, albeit on iPhone cases instead of the device itself.

items.title: Apple Store holiday return rules are in effect
items.content_html:
As it always does, in the run up to the holidays Apple has extended its return window. With some exceptions, buyers now have until early January 2027 to change their minds.

Apple does this every year, and each time the broad strokes are the same. From now until Christmas Day, most items can be returned until a date in early January.

For this year, Apple has announced that the return date is January 8, 2027. It has also, though, detailed what is excluded from that:

  • Apple Gift Cards
  • Apple developer membership and other products
  • Installed software or upgrades from the App Store

Most importantly, though, is what happens with the return of an iPhone or a cellular iPad, if it were bought locked to a particular carrier.

"Wireless carriers have different service-cancellation policies," notes Apple. "Returning your iPhone or iPad may not automatically cancel or reset your wireless account."

Consequently Apple says that you "are responsible for your wireless service agreement."

Note, too, that Apple's returns policy only applies to items bought from either a retail Apple Store or its online one. In the case of an online order, the date the product is received is used to determine eligibility, not the order day.

All of this is the same as before, except that Apple has added back in its rejection of gift cards which it omitted in 2025. For completeness, the terms and conditions still include references to opened software, decades since Apple sold any apps in boxes.

These are the terms as apply to US customers, although there are very similar ones for international buyers. There is also a series of additional returns steps for customers in Puerto Rico, which Apple details on its returns page.

items.title: HomePod mini 2 review - Six years later, not enough reasons to upgrade yet
items.content_html:
The $149 HomePod mini 2 sounds slightly better and offers expanded connectivity, but neither improvement gives existing owners a compelling reason to upgrade.

Six years after the original HomePod mini arrived, Apple's second-generation speaker brings more than a faster processor. New Mac audio capabilities, four-speaker surround sound for Apple TV 4K, and upgraded wireless hardware expand what the compact speaker can do beyond playing music.

The HomePod mini 2 launched on October 30, 2026, without Siri AI, one of its most anticipated features. Until Apple delivers that update, the newer model makes a stronger case for first-time buyers and people expanding their setups than for anyone replacing a perfectly good original.

SpecificationHomePod mini (2020)HomePod mini 2 (2026)
Launch price$99$149
ProcessorApple S5Apple S10
Audio hardwareFull-range driver, two passive radiatorsFull-range driver, two passive radiators
Computational audioReal-time tuningAdvanced real-time tuning
MicrophonesFourThree
Wi-FiWi-Fi 4Wi-Fi 6E
BluetoothBluetooth 5.0Bluetooth 6
SiriStandard SiriStandard Siri, Siri AI coming later
Mac audioStandard AirPlayPersistent connection with compatible Macs
Apple TV surroundStandard playback and stereo pairingFour-speaker surround with fourth-generation Apple TV 4K
Stereo pairingTwo original minisTwo mini 2 speakers
Sound GlowSupported with software 27.2Supported
Smart homeApple Home hub, Thread, temperature and humidity sensorsApple Home hub, Thread, temperature and humidity sensors
Ultra WidebandYesYes
Dimensions3.3 x 3.9 inches3.3 x 3.9 inches
Weight0.76 pound0.74 pound
ColorsWhite, blue, orange, yellow, midnightWhite, blue, pink, green, midnight

The spec upgrades look great in a vacuum. It all comes down to how it works together, though, to deliver music.

Better sound, but not a dramatic improvement

The HomePod mini 2 delivered clear, balanced sound throughout our testing, with excellent room coverage and plenty of volume for everyday listening. Our initial comparison with the original HomePod mini didn't reveal much difference.

A second round of testing with lossless music brought out a modest improvement.

We listened to classical, metal, and dubstep to hear how the device handled different instruments, arrangements, and musical styles. With lossless playback enabled, the HomePod mini 2 offered slightly better instrument separation, making individual sounds easier to distinguish.

The improvement was noticeable when we listened closely, although it wasn't dramatic enough to change the overall experience. The original HomePod mini still sounds remarkably good for its size, and the newer model doesn't leave its predecessor behind.

Our speaker comparison examines how the two generations stack up, including their audio performance and connectivity.

The HomePod mini 2 also maintained consistent sound quality across the locations we tested. We could move the speaker between shelves, tables, and other convenient spots without losing the clarity or room coverage we enjoyed.

Apple continues to use a full-range driver and two passive radiators, with computational audio adjusting playback in real time. The newer S10 processor has considerably more processing power than the original S5, although both generations retain the same general speaker configuration.

The HomePod mini 2 delivered clear, balanced sound throughout our testing, with excellent room coverage and plenty of volume for everyday listening.

The HomePod mini 2's improved instrument separation gives it a small but welcome advantage, particularly for listeners who pay attention to the finer details of their music. For everyone else, the original still delivers much of the same listening experience without requiring another purchase.

Familiar design with a faster processor

Anyone familiar with the original HomePod mini will recognize the second-generation model immediately. Apple has kept the rounded, mesh-covered design and illuminated touch surface, with controls for playback and volume on top.

The HomePod mini 2 measures 3.3 inches tall and 3.9 inches wide, making it easy to fit on a desk, shelf, or bedside table. Apple has refreshed the color selection with pink and green, replacing the original generation's orange and yellow options alongside blue, white, and midnight.

Inside, the S10 replaces the original S5 processor, while Wi-Fi improves from Wi-Fi 4 to Wi-Fi 6E. Bluetooth also moves from version 5.0 to Bluetooth 6, with Thread networking and Ultra Wideband support carrying over from the original.

The faster processor brings more potential benefits than just audio processing. Separate hands-on testing found that Siri responded more quickly and Handoff transferred audio faster than on the original HomePod mini.

I should rename the HomePod mini 2 to The Eye of Sauron

There's also an important limitation for anyone planning to mix old and new HomePods. Apple requires two speakers of the same model and generation for stereo pairing, so an original HomePod mini can't form a stereo pair with a HomePod mini 2.

If you already own one original HomePod mini and want stereo sound, you'll need to find another first-generation model or purchase two newer speakers. You can't mix generations.

Sound Glow isn't exclusive to the new speaker

Sound Glow gives the HomePod mini 2's illuminated touch surface a more colorful appearance during music playback. The lighting draws colors from album artwork and pulses along with the music, adding a little movement to an otherwise understated design.

You won't need a new HomePod mini to enjoy the effect, though. Apple also brought Sound Glow to the original HomePod mini and second-generation HomePod through HomePod software 27.2.

The lighting is a welcome visual addition, especially if your speaker sits somewhere visible while you're listening. Since existing HomePods support the same feature, Sound Glow doesn't provide much incentive to upgrade.

Siri AI remains the biggest missing feature

Siri AI could eventually become one of the HomePod mini 2's biggest improvements, but the upgraded assistant still isn't available on the speaker as of November 4, 2026.

Apple has promised more natural conversations, broader knowledge, and better music discovery, along with requests that use personal information from supported apps. Users will eventually be able to ask Siri to find a song mentioned in a message or create a reminder using information stored elsewhere on their devices.

The expanded capabilities could make Siri more useful for everyday requests, especially when a command involves information spread across different apps. For now, HomePod mini 2 owners are still working with the existing assistant, and Apple hasn't announced a specific release date for the upgrade.

Getting the new Siri features will also involve more than updating the speaker. The home owner will need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad running compatible software, with Siri AI enabled.

Requests involving personal context will require a paired compatible device, although other household members will be able to use some conversational and knowledge features without owning one themselves.

Siri AI has the potential to make the HomePod mini 2 more appealing, particularly for households that rely heavily on voice commands. Until Apple releases the update, though, we can't judge how accurately the assistant responds or how much its new abilities improve daily use.

We'll be re-reviewing the HomePod Mini 2 when it launches.

Four-speaker surround sound comes at a price

The HomePod mini 2 also supports a new four-speaker surround sound arrangement when paired with the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K. The system uses matching front and rear speaker pairs, automatically adjusting audio timing and levels based on their positions in the room.

You can build the setup using four HomePod mini 2 speakers or combine two minis with two second-generation full-sized HomePods. The arrangement offers another option for Apple TV owners who want something more immersive than a traditional stereo pair.

We couldn't test the four-speaker surround sound setup because we don't have a new Apple TV 4K yet. We'll take a closer look at surround sound pairing and its performance in our upcoming Apple TV 4K review.

Building a setup from scratch also requires a considerable investment. Four HomePod mini 2 speakers cost $596, and the new Apple TV 4K is priced at $299, bringing the minimum total to $895 before tax.

Our earlier surround comparison explores alternative speaker systems available for less money.

Siri AI has the potential to make the HomePod mini 2 more appealing.

For someone who already owns compatible HomePods, the new arrangement could be worth exploring when the required Apple TV arrives. Anyone buying all the hardware specifically for surround sound should compare the complete system with other home theater options before spending nearly $900.

Smart home features remain familiar

The HomePod mini 2 continues to serve as an Apple Home hub, giving users a way to control compatible accessories and run automations. Thread networking and built-in temperature and humidity sensors also remain available for smart home setups.

Anyone upgrading from the original HomePod mini will already have access to those features. Apple's first-generation speaker supports the same basic smart home capabilities, so the newer model doesn't fundamentally change what you can control.

For someone starting an Apple Home setup, the HomePod mini 2 still offers a useful combination of smart speaker and home hub. Existing owners can continue using their original HomePods for most of the same tasks.

HomePod mini 2 is better for new buyers than existing owners

The HomePod mini 2 delivers good sound with excellent room coverage and enough volume for everyday listening. Our lossless comparison revealed slightly better instrument separation than the original, giving the newer speaker a modest but noticeable audio advantage.

Apple has also expanded what the speaker can do beyond playing music. Persistent Mac audio and four-speaker surround sound could make the HomePod mini 2 more useful in different parts of the home, although neither feature has been fully evaluated in our testing.

Siri AI remains another potentially significant improvement, but you shouldn't base the purchase on an assistant update that hasn't arrived.

At $149, we'd recommend the HomePod mini 2 more readily to someone buying their first HomePod or expanding an existing setup than to someone replacing a working original.

If you already own a HomePod mini and primarily use it for music, Siri commands, and Apple Home, you'll get slightly better sound and newer hardware by upgrading. The improvements are welcome, but they aren't substantial enough to justify replacing speakers that already do their jobs well.

HomePod mini 2 pros

  • Clear, balanced sound
  • Better instrument separation with lossless music
  • Excellent room coverage
  • Updated wireless connectivity and expanded audio options
  • Useful Apple Home hub functionality

HomePod mini 2 cons

  • Modest audio improvements over the original HomePod mini
  • Siri AI isn't available at launch
  • Can't create a stereo pair with the original HomePod mini
  • Four-speaker surround requires expensive additional hardware

Score: 3 out of 5

The HomePod mini 2 is a product in the midst of becoming more. Siri AI may change it enough to justify a higher score, and surround sound pairing on Apple TV hardware may too.

We'll see. Like I said before, we'll re-review when Siri AI works on the model.

For now, if you have an original HomePod mini, stick with that. There's not enough justification to pay more for functionality you have right now.

Where to buy the HomePod mini 2

Apple's HomePod mini 2 retails for $149 and can be ordered at B&H Photo, Expercom, and Adorama.

items.title: New Apple Music Classical update matches wider Music rebrand

Classical music doesn't always fit into the traditional album-based framework of most music apps, something the Apple Music Classical app counters with a bespoke design.

Apple Music Classical plays host to a wide array of music

The newly updated app builds on the previous Liquid Glass update that arrived alongside iOS 26 in 2025. It now more closely matches the rest of Apple's first-party offerings, especially Apple Music.

The newly updated app is available for download from the App Store now. Apple Music Classical is included as part of the Apple Music subscription at no extra cost, and has its own apps across Apple's platforms.

items.title: Apple's bond sale is now confirmed at $7.5 billion
items.content_html:
Details of Apple's expected bond sale have now been confirmed in SEC filings, which show the company aims to raise a slightly higher than expected $7.5 billion.

It had been reported that Apple was aiming to raise around $7 billion through this bond offering, which is the sale of debt. That report was based on a preliminary filing with the SEC, but now the final pricing term sheet has been published.

This filing confirms that Apple plans to issue bonds in seven series that would mature between 2028 and 2036:

  • 2028: $500 million in floating-rate bonds plus $1 billion in fixed-rate bonds with a 4.65% annual interest rate
  • 2029: $750 million in floating-rate bonds plus $1 billion in fixed-rate bonds with a 4.75% annual interest rate
  • 2031: $1 billion in fixed-rate bonds with a 4.90% annual interest rate
  • 2033: $1.25 billion in fixed-rate bonds with a 5.10% annual interest rate
  • 2036: $2 billion in fixed-rate bonds with a 5.35% annual interest rate

Those floating-rate bonds will be at interest rates tied to the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), which is adjusted every quarter. The fixed-rate notes are obviously constant.

What Apple gets

While the filing is for $7.5 billion, Apple actually expects to get around $7.47 billion. That's accounting for various costs and discounts.

Apple has filed that it intends the proceeds to be spent on "general corporate purposes, including repurchases of our common stock and payment of dividends under our program to return capital to shareholders, funding for working capital, capital expenditures, acquisitions and repayment of debt."

There is no breakdown of what proportion of the $7.47 billion will be spent on any of these areas.

items.title: Democrat orders Apple to disclose details of Trump ballroom donation
items.content_html:
Tech companies including Apple have been told to turn over documentation regarding donations to the Trump ballroom, and threatened with subpoenas if they do not.

It's previously been reported that Apple donated $25 million to Trump's planned ballroom at the White House. Now following the midterms, such donations will be examined by the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations under its new Democrat leader, Senator Richard Blumenthal.

According to Reuters, the senator called on Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and others to turn over their records. Right now this is voluntary, but when Blumenthal takes the leadership position in January 2027, the firms will likely be compelled under subpoena.

It's not the first time that Senator Blumenthal has raised the issue, as he wrote to certain firms about donations in 2025. "Many of the donors have deep financial, business, or other personal interests before the Administration," he wrote.

Reportedly, firms presumably including Apple did not respond to that letter, and the administration has ignored similar requests.

Senator Blumenthal has also called on FCC Chair Brendan Carr to disclose details of decisions including the Paramount Skydance merger. He criticized Carr's ordering an early license review of Disney's ABC-owned stations.

Blumenthal said that Carr's actions "erode and undermine freedom of speech and freedom of the press and bear on the laws governing media consolidation."

Referring to both Carr and the tech companies, he also said if documentation is not provided, "it will leave the subcommittee with no choice but to consider alternative measures to obtain compliance."

What happens next

Whether Apple discloses details voluntarily now or under subpoena in January, the subcommittee will clearly receive details of the donation. However, it's hard to see quite what those details can be beyond confirmation of the $25 million amount.

Then since there has already been demolishing work and some construction on the ballroom, it's unlikely that the project will be cancelled. Conceivably, the donations could be returned to the companies, but then the committed sums would have to come from the public purse.

What this will really achieve is to put a spotlight on just how Apple and others have been compelled to support the Trump administration. Trump himself has previously boasted about having Tim Cook "kiss my ass" to avoid certain extra tariffs, amongst other issues.

The demands of the administration were always going to be questioned the next time there was a Democrat President, or when Democrats took sufficient control of the house and senate. This may be why Tim Cook chose to make a personal donation to Trump's inauguration instead of Apple.

items.title: How to dim or turn off the glowing Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro
items.content_html:
Apple has returned the glowing white Apple logo to the lid of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR. It's not in Settings, but there's a way to turn it off.

You just can't please people. For ten years we've been denied the once famous glowing logo and as soon as we get it back, there are complaints.

There are people who want the newest iPhones to come in distinctive colors just so that everyone knows they've got the latest one. So you'd think there'd also be people who'd want you to know they've got — and could afford — the new MacBook Pro.

But whether it's they don't want to advertise Apple quite so visibly, or whether they want to pretend to be using Windows laptops, there is a solution. Actually, there are two solutions, where one is Apple just accepting the physics of the situation, and the other is it making you work for what you want.

The simple solution

The logo isn't how it used to be. The old version used the LCD backlight to illuminate a plastic cut out. OLED lighting doesn't work that way.

Instead, the logo is similar to how a smart light works. Brightness is tied to, but not because of, the main screen's brightness. So, Apple has set it up so you can reduce the glow of that literal back light, by dimming the display.

It's definitely a simple way to cut down the glow, but it's unlikely to be practical. You need to set the front screen's brightness to whatever it is you need, you don't want to be peering at it.

So the alternative it is to turn off the glowing logo in software. While that isn't difficult, Apple has no interest in making it a tick box.

Turning off the logo

Instead, as revealed in Apple's support documentation, the way to turn off the logo is to enter a Terminal command. Specifically paste this into Terminal:

sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0

You'll then be prompted to enter your Mac's password, but as soon as you've done that, the logo is off.

When you realize that you are missing out, though, you can go back to Terminal and instead paste in this:

sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode

The change is persistent, and will span all accounts on the Mac. Additionally, Apple notes that reinstalling macOS will also re-light the logo.

Another earnings call has come and gone, but this time it was CEO John Ternus at the helm. Sure, he read off prepared statements, but so has Tim Cook for every previous earnings call.

items.title: Apple is gearing up for a fresh $7 billion in bond sale
items.content_html:
Apple is reportedly seeking about $7 billion through a new bond offering, potentially raising more money for stock buybacks, dividends, and other corporate expenses.

A preliminary prospectus filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on November 5 confirms plans to issue seven series of bonds. However, the filing doesn't specify the total offering amount or final interest rates.

The offering would be Apple's first since May 2025, when it raised $4.5 billion through a four-part bond sale.

Apple's bond offering stretches through 2036

Apple's proposed offering includes two floating-rate notes maturing in 2028 and 2029, along with five fixed-rate notes due in 2028, 2029, 2031, 2033, and 2036.

The floating-rate notes will have interest rates tied to the Secured Overnight Financing Rate, or SOFR, with adjustments every quarter. Interest on the fixed-rate notes will remain constant and be paid twice a year.

Goldman Sachs, BofA Securities, Deutsche Bank Securities, and J.P. Morgan are managing the offering.

According to the SEC filing, Apple intends to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, including share repurchases, dividend payments, working capital, capital expenditures, acquisitions, and repayment of existing debt.

Apple hasn't disclosed how much it plans to spend on any particular purpose.

Why Apple is borrowing despite its cash flow

The proposed bond sale follows a strong financial quarter for Apple, which continues to generate substantial cash from its existing business. During its November 2 earnings announcement, the company reported record September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion and operating cash flow of $28 billion.

According to its annual report, Apple ended fiscal 2026 with $136.9 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities.

Operating cash flow reached $145.1 billion for the year, while spending on property and equipment totaled approximately $9 billion. After those expenditures, Apple had roughly $136.1 billion in free cash flow, far more than the $7 billion it's reportedly seeking.

The strong financial position suggests Apple isn't borrowing to cover immediate expenses. Additional debt could help preserve cash reserves while the company continues rewarding shareholders and funding other investments.

Shareholder returns remained substantial during fiscal 2026, with Apple repurchasing $85.8 billion in stock and paying another $15.7 billion in dividends and dividend equivalents. In April 2026, the company also authorized a new share repurchase program worth up to $100 billion.

However, shareholder returns aren't the only possible explanation for the borrowing. Apple also faces substantial debt repayments over the coming year, making refinancing another potential use for the proceeds.

As of September 26, 2026, Apple had $78.1 billion in outstanding unsecured senior notes and another $2 billion in short-term commercial paper. Its annual filing shows approximately $10 billion in existing bond principal coming due within 12 months, along with the $2 billion in commercial paper.

The new offering could help Apple manage those obligations without drawing as heavily on its cash reserves. However, the company hasn't indicated whether it intends to use the proceeds to refinance any specific debts.

The proposed sale also comes as other major technology companies turn to debt markets to finance expensive artificial intelligence infrastructure. Apple hasn't identified AI spending as a specific purpose for this offering, and its filing describes a much broader range of potential uses.

At the reported $7 billion, Apple's latest bond sale would be $2.5 billion larger than its May 2025 offering. The final amount and interest rates remain unsettled, but the company's financial position suggests the borrowing is more about maintaining flexibility than meeting an immediate funding need.

items.title: iPhone Duo brings multitasking to iPhone, but only just
items.content_html:
The iPhone Duo inner display brings multitasking to iPhone, but it stops just short of really turning Apple's first foldable into a multitasking monster. Here's how it works, and what the limitations are.

For years now, some of us have used iPhones as portable workstations thanks to big displays and super-fast chips. But the iPhone Duo takes things to a whole new level, whether you're working or having fun.

Apple's iPhone Duo multitasking isn't quite on par with an iPad thanks to the lack of windowing support, but two apps are better than one. And the large display means that those apps are still eminently usable, even taking up just one half of the available space.

So, let's going to dive into how multitasking works on the iPhone Duo. We'll look at what it can do and how it can be used so you know exactly what to expect from Apple's first foldable.

But we'll also take a look at the competition. Because no matter how great it is to use two apps in Split View, it would be even better if we could use three.

And yes, that's what you'll get elsewhere in the world of foldable phones.

Split-screen wonders

Running two apps side-by-side, called Split View, is a great way to make the most of the iPhone Duo's inner display. You can use any two apps, and some apps can even run twice, like Mail, Notes, and others that support multiple windows.

Doubling the number of apps, or windows, you can see at once might not double your productivity. But it sure does cut down on the constant app switching that comes with doing the same task on a traditional iPhone.

How you get into the iPhone Duo's Split View mode will depend on whether you're using two apps or two windows of the same app. Thankfully, both are intuitive and will become second nature in no time.

Two apps side-by-side

Opening two apps in Split View is almost as simple as opening one. You just have to do it twice.

  1. Open the first app that you want to use to get started. Now, swipe up from the bottom of the display and pause in the middle before dropping the app on the left or right side.
  2. The other side of the display will display your home screen. Tap the icon for the second app, and it will automatically open to fill the space.

Alternatively, tapping and holding on an app's icon on the home screen will reveal a new Open in Split View option. Tapping that will skip step one above, and you can tap the icon of your chosen second app as usual.

You can swap an app from one side to the other once you're in Split View. Just swipe up from the bottom of the app and drag it to the opposite side of the display.

If you have two apps that you regularly use together, you can pair them up. That way, tapping one of the apps' icons will automatically open both in Split View.

With both apps open in Split View, tap the divider between the two apps to lock them together. Unfortunately, as of iOS 27.2, there's no feedback that anything has happened.

Unpairing the two apps is as easy as dragging that divider to one side of the display, whether they're locked together or not.

Same app, two windows

Using two windows of the same app side-by-side can be useful when working in the Notes or Mail apps, for example. Being able to have two notes open at the same time, or writing one email while referencing another, can change your productivity game.

Multi-window support is something that's only available on an app-by-app basis, unfortunately. You'll unfortunately just have to try your most-used apps and cross your fingers.

Assuming the app does support multiple windows, the process of using them in Split View is similar to using two different apps.

  1. Tap and hold on the app's icon and choose Open in Split View to get started.
  2. Tap the app's icon again, this time on the side of the display that shows your home screen.

That's all there is to it, and we think you might be surprised how useful multi-window apps on the iPhone Duo can be. But there's also a secret third multitasking option.

Split-screen video

Like all iPhones, the iPhone Duo supports picture-in-picture when watching videos via supported apps. But the foldable goes a step further by offering to split the display for a more comfortable multitasking experience.

While Split View is only available in landscape orientation, this feature is the opposite. It only becomes available when watching a video in picture-in-picture mode in portrait.

The feature, which doesn't seem to have an actual name, locks the video in the top third of the display. The remaining two-thirds below it can then be used by another app.

There is a catch, however. That second app cannot be one that plays video. This isn't a way to watch two sports events at once.

But it does make it easier to keep up with your team's big game while scrolling your socials. And the feature is easy to use, too.

  1. Start playing a video in an app that supports picture-in-picture and tap the feature's icon. You'll be returned to the home screen with a floating video window, depending on the app. If not, swipe up to go home.
  2. With your iPhone Duo in portrait, open the app that you want to use at the bottom of the display.
  3. A new icon that looks like a display split into two sections will appear in the picture-in-picture window. Tap it to dock the video in the top third; the app will automatically fill the rest of the display.

This is a great way to watch a video while doing other things. Not least because it's much larger than the floating picture-in-picture window.

Those are all the options we have in terms of multitasking on an iPhone Duo. And while it's a huge improvement over any other iPhone, it can't keep up with the best in the business.

The multitasking monster

Apple's launch of the iPhone Duo in 2026 makes it a latecomer to the foldable market. Samsung wasn't the first, but it's been making foldables since 2019, and its multitasking features benefit from that fact.

The latest iterations, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra, really put the iPhone Duo's multitasking implementation in the shade. Two apps side-by-side is cool, but Samsung would argue that three is better.

That's exactly what you'll get if you use a Galaxy Z Fold 8 or Z Fold 8 Ultra. There are tools to adjust the size of the windows in ways Apple doesn't allow, and there are even floating windows if that's the route you want to take.

In short, Samsung's multitasking approach is much more akin to that of the iPad. Apple has chosen to go for a middle-ground approach, limiting the iPhone Duo to just two apps in Split View.

Apple's decision is unlikely to be down to processing power. The iPhone Duo uses the A20 Pro, the fastest chip ever to be placed into an iPhone.

Instead, it's more likely that Apple sees the iPhone Duo's display as too small to handle more than two apps at once. That, and it simply doesn't see the iPhone Duo as a multitasking device in the same way it does a big-screen iPad.

Whatever the reason, there's always a chance that Apple will unlock more multitasking features in the future. Annual iOS updates open that door, but it's impossible to know whether Apple intends to walk through it.

items.title: Instagram's Edits moves beyond the iPhone with Mac app
items.content_html:
Instagram is taking on CapCut on the Mac, expanding Edits beyond phones with tools for more involved video projects.

Instagram's free Edits video editor is now available for Mac, bringing a multi-track timeline, color controls, and direct Instagram publishing. The desktop app also supports horizontal and vertical videos, with watermark-free exports at up to 4K resolution.

The Mac version adds mouse and keyboard controls for projects that require more space than a phone screen provides. Users can also customize keyboard shortcuts, including matching those they use in another editor.

Editing tools include keyframes, audio waveforms, and controls for splitting, cutting, and trimming clips. Color wheels, log conversions, and curves handle color adjustments, while users can import their own LUTs and font files.

Edits features Instagram's licensed and royalty-free audio libraries, along with hundreds of sound and video effects. It also offers unlimited automatic captions with support for multiple languages.

Audio and text styles saved on mobile carry over to the desktop app. While not currently available, Instagram plans on making cross-platform editing available in the future.

Users can publish directly to Instagram from the Mac app, with support for tagging, locations, and trial reels. Export options also let users prepare videos for other platforms or personal projects.

The app includes an option to enable Model Context Protocol, or MCP, in settings for workflows involving AI agents. Instagram says it plans to release desktop updates weekly.

Edits for Mac is available to download starting Thursday. Currently, there is no Windows version.

Edits is a direct competitor to ByteDance's CapCut, which released its own macOS version in 2021. According to Meta's most recent earnings call, Edits already has more than 50 million active users.

items.title: PROLED touchscreen MacBook Pro review roundup: fantastic screen, touch is secondary
items.content_html:
The first reviews of the new MacBook Pro PROLED with touch display are out. All of them rave about the screen, just about all of wince at the price, and most shrug about touch.

Apple says these are the best MacBooks it's ever made, but it always says that. It says these have touch screens, and it's always rejected saying that.

Now that the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR models are in reviewers' hands, there is much talk of how Steve Jobs hated touch screens. Some like iJustine say he had a point, but all say what John Ternus has about this being the right time to add touch.

Then all of the reviews so far are incredible raves with barely any criticism. Except none of them give more than passing attention to the touch screen.

Mashable

"It's brilliant in every way," says Mashable in its review. "It also has a touch screen, which is fine."

Calling it "the first slam dunk of the Ternus era," the review insists that "what's really exciting about this new Apple machine is the incredible tandem OLED display." It even says that Apple "wasn't exaggerating" with its claims of having an industry-leading display.

"This laptop absolutely slaps, and the incredible PROLED XDR display is the headline," concludes the reviewer. "It's stunning."

Tom's Guide

On YouTube, Tom's Guide says that touch "is the flashy headline this year," but that it's the screen that matters.

"I'm just going to say it upfront, this is the best laptop display I have ever tested," continues the review.

PC Magazine

Out of reviews so glowing that they could've been written by Apple, PC Magazine's tiny criticism seems loud. It says that this "is a slightly more powerful laptop" than the most recent update.

It comes with "some quirks: loud cooling fans under load," says the review, "and an easy-to-smudge screen (unless you pony up for Apple's nano-texture panel upgrade."

But then the review summarizes the new MacBook Pro by saying that "'premium doesn't begin to cover it." And that this is the "new bar for laptop touch screens."

Even that is less about touch, though, and more because the screen is "one of the first (if not the first) reference grade" display in a laptop. PC Magazine gives the new MacBook Pro 4.5 stars and an Editor's Choice award.

Trusted Reviews

It might be a lesser-known source for Apple users, but Trusted Reviews is as enthused as everyone else. It's also enthused in exactly the same way, saying that there's now touch, but that it's the display "that I am more ecstatic about."

"OLED displays aren't new on laptops — they're pretty common on Windows machines, even more affordable ones — but this is the first time there has been one on a Mac," it continues. "And it's fantastic."

Gizmodo

The Gizmodo review cuts straight to the point with its headline: "Screw touchscreens, it's still the best Mac." While it does praise the touch feature, it concludes that "you're not going to end up using a touch display all too often."

Unlike most reviews that concentrate on display or touch, Gizmodo also wants to enthuse about audio. "The audio setup includes the same six speakers with four force-cancelling woofers," it says, "but the upgraded drivers on the models offer a sound quality that is much cleaner than before."

"[This] may become my favorite device for all sorts of content," it concludes.

items.title: How to install macOS Tahoe on unsupported Macs
items.content_html:
With OpenCore Legacy Patcher, now on version 3, you can get macOS Tahoe running on Intel Macs released more than fifteen years ago. Here's how to get everything set up.

Though Apple Silicon Macs have already moved on to macOS Golden Gate, the preceding macOS Tahoe remains a crucial update for older Apple computers. macOS Tahoe is the last release of macOS with support for Intel-based machines, running on select Macs released in 2019 and 2020.

Owners of older hardware were simply out of luck, until now. With Dortania's OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0, a prominent third-party solution, it's possible to run macOS Tahoe on a variety of unsupported Macs, including models over a decade and a half old.

At the time of writing, version 3.0.0 of the OpenCore Legacy Patcher is still in the release candidate stage. This means that, although macOS Tahoe will likely run on your older Mac, you might encounter difficulties installing it, and you might experience bugs in the OS itself.

Nonetheless, OCLP remains as significant as it has ever been for owners of vintage Apple hardware. With it, you can get new software features and web browsers on machines Apple has given up on altogether.

The patcher uses the OpenCore bootloader to "inject and patch data in memory instead of on disk." According to the OCLP GitHub page, this is why the patcher can achieve near-native levels of performance on officially unsupported Apple hardware.

OpenCore is a so-called custom bootloader, loaded before the main operating system. It's an open-source project, available on acidanthera's GitHub page. At startup, it lets you select between one or more operating systems currently installed.

On its own, OpenCore is commonly used in the Hackintosh community, where people install macOS on non-Apple PCs. This guide, however, focuses only on OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0 and how to use it to install macOS Tahoe on genuine, unsupported Mac computers. No prior knowledge is necessary, apart from basic familiarity with macOS.

Before upgrading to macOS Tahoe, it's important to understand which operating systems and Mac models are compatible with Dortania's OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0.

Which versions of macOS can you run with OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0.0?

OpenCore Legacy Patcher lets you install any version from macOS Big Sur to macOS Tahoe on select unsupported machines. Version 3.0.0 introduced macOS Tahoe support, while older builds of the patcher only support macOS Big Sur through macOS Sequoia.

For older versions of macOS, AppleInsider suggests checking out dosdude1's Catalina patcher. NexPostFacto is great for even older Mac computers that can't officially run macOS Mavericks, like the original Intel iMac from 2006.

At the time of writing, OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0.0 is primarily intended for use with macOS Tahoe 26.7, macOS 26.7.1, and macOS 26.7.2. As it currently stands, macOS Golden Gate support is neither planned nor feasible, since the update only supports Apple Silicon Macs.

Which Mac models are capable of running macOS Tahoe via OCLP?

According to the OpenCore Legacy Patcher GitHub page, the software makes it possible to run macOS Sequoia on the following unsupported Mac computers:

  • Late 2008 to 2017 13-inch and 12-inch MacBooks
  • Late 2008 to 2017 11-inch and 13-inch MacBook Airs
  • Early 2008 to 2017 13-inch, 15-inch and 17-inch MacBook Pros
  • Early 2009 to 2014 Mac minis
  • Mid-2007* to 2019* 20-inch to 27-inch iMacs
  • Early 2008 to 2013 Mac Pros
  • Early 2009 to 2011 XServe

Note that Mid-2007 iMac models require an upgraded CPU for use with OpenCore Legacy Patcher. These computers can be upgraded with either a T9300 2.5 GHz Intel Core 2 Duo or a T9500 2.6 GHz Intel Core 2 Duo. 2019 iMacs currently cannot boot into macOS Tahoe by default, but this issue is being worked on.

For Early 2009 through Mid 2011 iMacs, as well as Early 2008 and 2009 Xserve models, an upgrade to a Metal-compatible GPU is recommended for better graphics performance and graphics acceleration. Metal is Apple's GPU-accelerated graphics and compute framework, used throughout more recent versions of macOS.

Pre-2012 Macs typically lack a Metal-compatible GPU by default, though select iMac and XServe machines can be upgraded with newer graphics cards. OCLP still supports non-Metal Macs, but users will experience performance issues and Metal-related UI problems, such as the Photos app failing to load.

At the time of writing, Macs with a T2 security chip cannot be upgraded to macOS Tahoe or macOS Sequoia via OCLP. The following Macs are currently NOT compatible with OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0.0:

  • All 2018 and 2019 MacBook Pro models
  • All 2018 and 2019 MacBook Air models
  • 2017 iMac Pro

Due to an issue with the T2 chip, these Apple computers are stuck on older versions of macOS for the time being.

Preparing your Mac for macOS Tahoe

Before attempting to install an unsupported version of macOS, it's important to take a few precautions, and to ensure you have the equipment necessary to proceed.

As with every major software update, AppleInsider recommends that you make a backup of the most important data stored on your Mac. We also suggest using a form of portable flash storage media, such as an external solid-state drive (SSD), USB flash drive, or a large enough SD card. Alternatively, you can use cloud-based backup solutions or a mechanical hard drive.

While it may be tempting to try to install macOS Tahoe right away, it's best to first update your Mac to its last officially supported version. For a 2012 unibody MacBook Pro, for instance, this means updating the laptop to macOS Catalina.

For optimal performance, you'll also want to upgrade your Mac's hardware, if possible. On select Macs, the RAM, storage, CPU, and GPU can be upgraded. Ideally, your Mac should have at least 8GB of RAM and an internal solid-state drive (SSD) for use with macOS Tahoe.

Note that, with macOS Tahoe, Apple removed support for Fusion Drives, and OCLP 3.0.0 is not compatible with Fusion Drives, either. This type of drive is commonly found in base model Intel iMacs from the 2010s. If your Mac has a Fusion Drive, your best option is to replace it with an SSD.

Some of the oldest Macs supported by OCLP require wired peripherals during the macOS Tahoe installation process, even if they already have input devices. The built-in trackpad and keyboard on MacBook Pros from 2008 and 2009 are unusable while installing macOS 26, so you will need to connect a USB 1.1-compatible keyboard and mouse.

In short, this means you'll need an older keyboard and mouse to install macOS Tahoe on your MacBook Pro. From our testing, AppleInsider can confirm that the wired Apple Keyboard, model number A1243, from 2013, will get the job done. This particular keyboard has USB-A ports on its sides, which you can use to connect a wired mouse.

Next, make sure your Mac has an active internet connection via Ethernet, if it has a built-in port. Many older Macs capable of running macOS Tahoe with OCLP require root patches for wireless connectivity, meaning Wi-Fi isn't available during the macOS Tahoe installation and setup process.

Once you've prepared the necessary peripherals, backed up your data, updated your Mac to its last officially supported version, and ensured that your Mac can run macOS 26 via OCLP, you're ready to proceed.

For the next step, you will need a 32GB or larger USB flash drive, or an external SSD, as this is required to create a bootable macOS Tahoe installer with OpenCore Legacy Patcher. First, you will need to download the Patcher itself and a compatible Kernel Debug Kit.

Downloading and installing OpenCore Legacy Patcher, Apple's KDKs

You can download OpenCore Legacy Patcher version 3.0.0 from the releases section of Dortania's official GitHub page. From the page area labeled Assets, select OpenCore-Patcher.pkg, download the file, and install it.

After you've downloaded and installed the .pkg file, you can find the OpenCore Legacy Patcher app in your Applications folder. In theory, OCLP is the only software you should need to install and use macOS Tahoe, but in reality, you will likely need an additional resource from Apple itself.

For most older Macs, it's a good idea to download Apple's Kernel Debug Kit (KDK) for the operating system version you plan to install. KDKs for macOS 26.7, 26.7.1, and 26.7.2 are available on Dortania's GitHub page.

From the Assets tab, select the Kernel Debug Kit DMG file and download it. You will need the KDK after installing macOS Tahoe on your old Mac, as a prerequisite for root patching.

Older Macs will not have Wi-Fi immediately enabled after installing macOS Tahoe. This makes it difficult, if not impossible, to download the KDK needed for Wi-Fi patches and other features.

That's why having the proper KDK on a modern Mac, on a separate USB drive, SD card, or external SSD, will come in handy later on.

Once you've downloaded the proper KDK and OCLP, you're ready to make a macOS Tahoe installer with the OpenCore Legacy Patcher. Now, plug in the USB flash drive or external SSD you'll use to create a bootable macOS installer.

Creating a bootable macOS install drive with OpenCore Legacy Patcher

With OpenCore Patcher 3.0.0, the development team added a credits screen that appears whenever the patcher is launched for the first time. Scroll down until you see the Continue button, and click it.

After that, you'll be greeted with the patcher's main graphical user interface. OCLP includes a built-in option to create a bootable installer. Clicking the Create macOS Installer button will let you select the macOS version you wish to install.

The patcher can download macOS installer apps from the internet, or you can use a macOS Tahoe installer app you already downloaded beforehand. Direct download links for macOS installer packages can be found on Mr. Macintosh's website.

To download a macOS Installer package from the internet, click on Download macOS Installer.

The OpenCore Legacy Patcher will now present you with a list of different installers that can be downloaded. Choose macOS Tahoe 26.7, 26.7.1, or 26.7.2, the same version for which you downloaded a Kernel Debug Kit beforehand.

Once you have downloaded a macOS Tahoe installer, you can create a bootable macOS installer drive via the OpenCore Legacy Patcher app.

The OpenCore Legacy Patcher app will ask you to select a local disk. Select the USB drive or external solid-state drive you plugged in earlier.

The OpenCore Patcher will remind you that all data on this disk will be erased. This is necessary to create the macOS Tahoe installer, so click the Yes button.

The Patcher application will now start creating a bootable macOS installer. This step will take some time, depending on the speed of your external drive.

After the Patcher has created a bootable macOS installer, you will see a prompt asking you if you want to install OpenCore on this drive. You need to click Yes when this prompt shows up; otherwise, you won't be able to boot into the installer.

Now the OpenCore Legacy Patcher will start building the correct OpenCore configuration for your Mac. You will see a pop-up once this is finished. Click on Install to disk.

You will now have to select your external USB drive or solid-state drive. Do not select your Mac's main drive, or you will not be able to boot into the installer.

Then select the EFI of the external drive plugged into your Mac.

Once you've created a bootable macOS Tahoe installer with OpenCore installed on the external drive's EFI, connect a wired keyboard and mouse if you're using a 2008 or 2009 MacBook Pro. Then, you can click Reboot to restart your Mac.

Your Mac should then restart.

Installing macOS Tahoe

As soon as the Mac powers on, press and hold the Option or Alt key on your keyboard. A blank screen with multiple large icons will pop up. Use the arrow keys to select the EFI Boot option and press the Return key.

After doing so, you will see a second, similar screen. This time, you'll need to use the arrow keys to select Install macOS Tahoe and press the Return key.

Your computer should now boot into the macOS Tahoe installer from the external drive plugged in earlier. Note that with select older Macs, like 2008 and 2009 MacBook Pro models, the built-in keyboard and trackpad cannot be used during the macOS Tahoe installation process.

Consequently, you will need to navigate the necessary macOS Tahoe installer menus using the wired keyboard and mouse you plugged in earlier.

From here, you can install macOS Tahoe as you would normally, by simply selecting Install macOS Tahoe, agreeing to the license agreement, and selecting your Mac's internal drive as the location to install macOS Tahoe.

Doing so will install macOS Tahoe while preserving the data, applications, and settings you may already have on your Mac. Alternatively, you can also erase or partition your Mac's internal drive with Disk Utility, and then install a fresh copy of macOS Tahoe.

macOS Tahoe installation and setup process, known issues

Once you have accepted the terms of Apple's license agreement and chosen your Mac's internal drive, macOS Tahoe will begin installing.

During the process, your Mac should reboot multiple times. Do not interact with the Mac while it is installing macOS or while it's rebooting. Wait until the installer has finished before going back to the computer.

If your Mac has built-in fans, as is the case with MacBook Pro models, you may hear the fans turn on. This is normal during the installation process and is no cause for alarm.

After the installation is complete, if you chose to install macOS Tahoe on a blank drive or partition, you'll be greeted with a setup screen. Here you'll need to make a local user account and configure macOS Settings.

Note that many older Macs are extremely slow during the setup process, to the extent that they may appear unresponsive altogether. However, with enough patience, you will be able to complete most of the setup process.

Additionally, as internet access may not be available during the macOS Tahoe setup, you will need to configure your Apple Account and iCloud settings later. This does not mean your Mac has experienced a hardware failure and is, once again, no cause for alarm.

During the setup screen where you're meant to configure automatic update settings for macOS Tahoe, you will encounter a minor issue. At the time of writing, the macOS Tahoe Setup Assistant freezes once an update setting has been selected.

According to the OCLP development team, the Setup Assistant freezes because of the "Hello" screen that's supposed to follow. This screen is meant to be rendered using Metal, and given that Macs running OCLP don't have root patches at this stage, they can't load the "Hello" screen.

As a result, you will need to force reboot your Mac once the Install Assistant stops responding. To do so, simply hold the Power button for five seconds. Your Mac should shut down, and now you can boot it up normally.

What to do if your Mac is unreasonably slow right after installing macOS Tahoe

During the last phase of the macOS Tahoe installation process, OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0.0 attempts to automatically apply so-called "root patches."

These patches enable features such as Metal graphics acceleration, the keyboard backlight, built-in keyboard and trackpad, and more, depending on the model. However, release candidate builds of OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0.0 will not install the necessary root patches automatically.

This means that your Mac will be unreasonably slow and experience graphical glitches, including a gray dock, upon first using macOS Tahoe. With 2008 and 2009 MacBook Pro models, the integrated keyboard and trackpad are still non-functional at this stage, meaning you'll need to use wired peripherals.

Thankfully, there's an easy fix, where Apple's Kernel Debug Kit often comes into play.

Installing the Apple Kernel Debug Kit for macOS Tahoe

After booting into macOS Tahoe, transfer the OpenCore-Patcher.pkg file and the KDK you downloaded previously onto the drive with macOS Tahoe. Then, install both utilities.

macOS Tahoe will often refuse to open Apple's Kernel Debug Kit due to the operating system's security Settings. You might have to open System Settings > Privacy and Security, and scroll down to manually allow the KDK installer to open.

Once you've installed the correct KDK, you're ready to apply root patches to enable Wi-Fi, the keyboard, trackpad, and more hardware features, depending on your Mac model.

If the OpenCore Legacy Patcher prompts you to install root patches, click the OK button, followed by the Reboot button.

If this prompt does not appear, you will need to install the root patches manually.

Manually applying post-install root patches

Open the OCLP app and select Post-Install Root Patch. A post-install menu will pop up, informing you if any root patches are necessary.

If the description says anything other than "Revert first to update or reinstall OCLP," click the Start Root Patching button.

The OpenCore Legacy Patcher will identify your Mac model and apply the necessary root patches. Doing so will enable graphics acceleration and certain hardware components, depending on the Mac. In short, you should no longer see a gray dock after applying the root patches and restarting.

Once the root patches have been installed, the OpenCore Legacy Patcher will ask if you want to reboot your Mac. Click Reboot. After this, you should not experience graphical issues anymore.

After you have applied the post-install root patches, you need to install OpenCore on your Mac's internal drive so that your computer can boot without the external installer drive.

Installing the OpenCore bootloader on your Mac's internal drive

Currently, your Mac uses the OpenCore bootloader installed on the external drive, which was used to install macOS Tahoe. This means your Mac cannot boot into its new operating system unless the drive is connected.

To remove this requirement, you'll need to install OpenCore on the internal drive of your Mac, the same drive or partition where macOS Tahoe was just installed.

The OpenCore Legacy Patcher application will typically notify you if you're using OpenCore from an external drive. It will offer to install OpenCore on your Mac's internal storage. Click on OK if you see a prompt about this.

This will start building an OpenCore configuration for your Mac. If the previous prompt doesn't appear, you can build OpenCore manually. To do this, open the OpenCore Legacy Patcher app and select Build and install OpenCore.

After an OpenCore configuration has been created, click on Install to disk.

The patcher will ask you to select a local disk. Choose your Mac's internal drive and not the external USB or solid-state drive.

After this, you'll need to select the internal drive's EFI and install OpenCore onto it. Once this is done, eject and unplug the external drive, and reboot your Mac as instructed by the OpenCore Legacy Patcher app.

As soon as your Mac turns on, press and hold the Option or Alt key. Use the arrow keys to select the EFI Boot icon, and press the Return key. Your Mac should now be able to boot into macOS Tahoe directly from the internal drive.

Disabling automatic downloads for software updates

Once you have successfully installed macOS Tahoe, and once your Mac can boot into the operating system without any issues, you're ready to move to the next step.

Open System Settings, navigate to General > Software Update.

After this, click the i icon next to the Automatic Updates setting. Make sure that all of the options listed here are disabled.

Disabling these automatic downloads significantly reduces the chances of experiencing issues with your operating system in the future. Your Mac will not be able to, for instance, install a new operating system update that is incompatible with the version of OpenCore Legacy Patcher currently installed.

Performance and overall usability of macOS Tahoe on unsupported hardware

You should now have a Mac that runs macOS Tahoe without any major issues. However, many of the machines supported by OpenCore Legacy Patcher debuted over a decade and a half ago, and it shows when using macOS Tahoe.

With older hardware, the performance obviously won't be up to par with officially supported machines, especially those with an M1 or newer chip. The main issue with macOS Tahoe on unsupported Macs is the time the machines take to get ready for use.

Even on computers with Metal-capable graphics cards, it still takes about a minute until all macOS Tahoe user interface elements fully load. On Macs that support Metal, boot times are similar to macOS Sequoia.

On Metal-capable machines, such as the 2012 MacBook Pro, performance is on par with macOS Sequoia, and possibly even better. While perhaps not ideal, macOS Tahoe is perfectly usable on this machine. Performance will obviously still vary depending on your Mac's specific hardware, and whether or not it's been upgraded.

When it comes to older Macs without a Metal-compatible GPU, however, such as the 2008 or 2009 MacBook Pro models, the situation is substantially different. Even with an SSD and 8GB of RAM, you will still have to wait about five minutes for macOS Tahoe to become usable.

Even that usability is questionable, as you will find yourself waiting minutes for select apps or UI elements to load. In short, macOS Tahoe is usable on non-Metal Macs only if you have the patience of a saint.

Worse yet, many unsupported Macs don't get all the bells and whistles Apple announced with macOS Tahoe or even macOS Sequoia, as most new capabilities are hardware-specific.

Siri AI and Apple Intelligence are not available on unsupported Macs or Intel Macs

The main drawback of using an older Mac on Tahoe is the lack of Apple Intelligence. Intel-based Macs, even those officially supported by Apple, do not feature Apple Intelligence as they lack the necessary hardware.

Apple Intelligence is the name used for Apple's generative AI feature suite, which lets users edit images and text and summarize emails or conversations with the help of artificial intelligence.

Macs with an Intel processor don't have a neural processing unit or NPU, which is needed for Apple Intelligence. Only Mac computers with an M1 or newer Apple Silicon chip feature an NPU, which Apple calls the Neural Engine.

As a result, users of older, Intel-based Mac computers cannot access any of Apple's more recent AI features. No Apple Intelligence capabilities, be they from macOS Tahoe or macOS Sequoia, are available on Macs using OCLP.

Siri AI isn't available on Intel-based Macs either. The upgraded virtual assistant is offered only on macOS 27, an update exclusive to Apple Silicon Macs. At the time of writing, there are no indications to suggest Apple Intelligence or Siri AI can be ported to Macs with an Intel processor.

iPhone Mirroring will not work on older Macs without a T2 security chip

With macOS Sequoia, Apple introduced the "iPhone Mirroring" app, which lets you mirror the screen of your iPhone on your Mac. On officially supported Macs and iPhones, you can use this feature to easily drag and drop files between the two devices as well.

Apple's iPhone Mirroring application unfortunately has a hardware-based requirement. For the feature to work, an Intel Mac needs to have a T2 security chip. Many older Mac models supported by OpenCore Legacy Patcher do not feature a T2 security chip, making iPhone Mirroring impossible on these computers.

MacBook Pro and MacBook Air models from 2018 and 2019 all feature the T2 security chip required for iPhone Mirroring, as is the case with the 2017 iMac Pro. However, macOS Tahoe cannot be installed on these machines with OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0.0. Apple does not offer macOS Tahoe support for these computers, either.

Issues with Non-Metal Macs

Most Pre-2012 Macs lack a Metal-compatible graphics card. Simply put, Metal is a hardware-specific graphics acceleration framework that's used throughout macOS.

OpenCore Legacy Patcher's developers have created root patches specifically for non-Metal Macs. Users of older Mac computers will still be able to use macOS Tahoe without major problems, assuming they have the patience to wait for everything to load.

Additionally, non-Metal Macs may experience issues with features such as Tiled windows and Stage Manager. On these machines, the new Journal app is only partly functional, and it crashes whenever you attempt to make a new entry, while the Games and Maps apps crash upon launch.

Apps such as Photos and Weather also may not work properly on non-Metal machines running macOS Tahoe. Macs without a Metal-capable GPU also experience significant lag caused by the new wallpapers found in macOS Tahoe. Reverting to older macOS wallpapers, or using OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0.0 RC5 solves the issue.

At the time of writing, the OCLP development team notes that web views are broken on select non-Metal Macs, meaning the patcher's credits screen won't always load properly. The screen can be skipped before graphics patches are applied, though.

The official OpenCore Legacy Patcher GitHub page has a list of known problems affecting Macs without a Metal-compatible GPU. There are issues affecting two Metal-compatible Macs as well, with the 2019 iMac being unable to boot into Tahoe, and corrupted graphics plaguing the 2015 12-inch MacBook.

With the 2012 MacBook Pro we used for testing, we encountered a recurring issue where the keyboard and trackpad became unresponsive. This happened whenever we tried to log back into macOS after the laptop had entered sleep mode. Force-rebooting solves the issue temporarily.

Version 3.0.0 of the OpenCore Legacy Patcher is still in the release candidate stage, so some of these issues will likely be addressed in the future. Even in its current state, however, OCLP 3.0.0 helps old Macs learn some new tricks.

Liquid Glass, iPhone Calls, and other features you get with macOS Tahoe

While Apple Intelligence, Siri AI, and iPhone Mirroring are unavailable on unsupported Macs, you'll still get to enjoy many of the other enhancements found within macOS Tahoe, including Liquid Glass.

Introduced at WWDC 2026, Liquid Glass is Apple's latest user interface overhaul, with a glass-like design replacing the flat aesthetic used from macOS Yosemite through macOS Sequoia. Countless UI elements have been redesigned to resemble rounded glass objects.

You'll see the change right from the Lock Screen clock, through the Menu Bar and Control Center, down to the Dock and its icons. Application windows have more rounded corners, while buttons and sliders have different, more bouncy animations.

This, of course, has its downsides, as the new UI takes a lot longer to load on both Metal and non-Metal Macs. It appears as though the new design does take a slight toll on performance as well, though not to the point where it makes things unusable.

LaunchPad, meanwhile, has been replaced with the Apps view, effectively an app library of sorts. In our opinion, the change is a downgrade, as the new UI element takes longer to load and makes it difficult to find applications. For some reason, we also saw some system apps appear twice.

Speaking of apps, macOS Tahoe delivers three completely new ones: the Journal, Games, and Phone applications. While the Journal and Games apps don't work on non-Metal Macs, we've found that the Phone app lets you make phone calls even on non-Metal Macs.

The Games app, as its name implies, is meant to house your Mac's video game library. It also offers access to Apple Arcade titles, as well as Game Center integration. Apple's new game-focused app is a great addition, though you might not get much use out of it on Macs with dated hardware.

Apple's Journal app, meanwhile, offers an experience similar to the Notes application. You can log your thoughts, ideas, plans, daily schedules, and so on, and it even works with iCloud. Again, however, you won't get to use these without a Metal-compatible GPU.

Safari 26 and Safari 27, meanwhile, run on both Metal and non-Metal Macs, meaning you'll get access to Apple's latest version of WebKit. This comes in handy for modern websites, which increasingly require newer and newer web browsers.

Additional resources for installing macOS Tahoe on unsupported Macs

While this guide presents a basic overview of the macOS Tahoe installation process, it is by no means all-encompassing. That is why we recommend checking the official Dortania OpenCore Legacy Patcher GitHub page.

The page, from the developers themselves, includes a detailed guide and numerous useful resources. It also details the individual issues that affect specific unsupported Mac models and lists potential workarounds for some of them.

Note, however, that OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0.0 is still in the release candidate stage, meaning the development team will not offer assistance with installing macOS Tahoe just yet.

For those who prefer guides in video form, Mr. Macintosh has a dedicated video on installing macOS Tahoe via the OpenCore Legacy Patcher on unsupported Macs. Anson Alexander also has a similar video on his channel.

While there are plenty of useful resources and videos detailing the installation process, there are other factors that need to be taken into account. Before upgrading, you'll want to consider everything you'd get with macOS Tahoe and how it would impact your Mac in the long run.

Is macOS Tahoe worth running on unsupported Macs?

By installing macOS Tahoe on an unsupported Mac with a Metal-compatible GPU, you're effectively extending its lifespan well into the near future. Over time, an increasing number of third-party applications will likely require macOS Tahoe to run.

Updating to macOS Tahoe will also give you a better web browsing experience, given that you'll be using the latest version of Safari currently available. Outdated web browsers are a serious hindrance for older Mac computers, as pages will often fail to load properly or at all.

You'll also get to experience and take advantage of the many new apps and features found within macOS Tahoe, such as the Journal, Games, and Phone applications. It's impressive that the iPhone Calling feature still works on computers from 2009.

However, when it comes to non-Metal Macs on macOS Tahoe in general, the experience is less than ideal, to say the least. The Journal, Games, and Maps apps do not work on Macs without a Metal-compatible graphics card, so you won't get much beyond Safari 27 and the new Phone app.

With enough patience, you can use macOS Tahoe on a non-Metal Mac, though you'll probably want to keep it on a separate volume or partition. Older macOS releases, like macOS Monterey, are a much better option for computers with non-Metal graphics cards and dual-core CPUs.

If you have a Mac from 2012 and later, though, and you want to get the absolute most out of it, then OCLP is definitely worth considering. The features it enables with macOS Tahoe on Metal-compatible Macs make the OpenCore Legacy Patcher a worthwhile option.

items.title: Labrinth promotes PROLED MacBook Pro with an all-night music-making stream
items.content_html:
Multi-platinum musician Labrinth will be putting the PROLED MacBook Pro through its paces ahead of launch, using it to produce a full song from scratch on a live stream.

Apple's MacBook Pro with a Tandem OLED screen, referred to as PROLED, is coming out on November 6. As part of its promotion for the new model's launch, Apple is collaborating with a musical artist on an interesting live stream.

As hinted at on TikTok, Labrinth will be working through the night at the Tower Theater Apple Store in Downtown L.A. to create a new song from scratch. This will be completed on the new Mac notebook, as well as Apple's Logic Pro software.

Labrinth is a multi-platinum-selling singer, songwriter, and producer. Aside from solo hits like "Jealous" and "Earthquake," he is also part of the LSD supergroup with Sia and Diplo, and has collaborated with Beyonce on the Grammy-nominated "Spirit."

He has also served as a composer for the TV show "Euphoria," writing and performing the finale-capping song "All For Us." It won an Emmy for Outstanding Original Music and Lyrics.

The entire song-production process will be livestreamed on Labrinth's YouTube account, which has over 3.2 million subscribers, in real time. The live stream will start on November 4th at 8 P.M. Pacific, 11 P.M. Eastern.

The song itself will be released the following week, presumably through Apple Music.

items.title: First public betas for iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 are available
items.content_html: It's been a few days since the first developer beta of iOS 27.3, et al, and now, the public beta versions are available to download. We've hit a few bugs, and some incompatibilities, so if you have something mission-critical you rely on, maybe wait a bit.
